title_original: K-art, William Kentridge and a Turner prize worth getting excited for – the week in art
excerpt_original: Korean art rewinds 2,000 years, Kentridge enters another dimension and Rodinesque ghosts make a bid for art’s most prestigious gong – all in your weekly dispatch Turner prize Kira Freije creates a waste land peopled by Rodinesque ghosts in the machine, Simeon Barclay meditates…

blocks.text: Exhibition of the week

Turner prize Kira Freije creates a waste land peopled by Rodinesque ghosts in the machine, Simeon Barclay meditates on masculinity, Tanoa Sasraku takes on big oil and Marguerite Humeau gets lost in wonderland in the most exciting Turner prize in years. Image of the week

blocks.alt: Nicole Eisenman’s Parking Lot of Violent Forces and Depressive Positions, 2026.
blocks.caption: Photograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, London

blocks.text: Goons in the military fatigues and wraparound shades beloved of ICE agents ride around in a clown car – a pretty clear comment on contemporary US. Elsewhere a solitary figure amid the ruins of Stonehenge is overwhelmed by the universe – are we now lost in in cosmic speculation? Welcome to the abstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling world of Nicole Eisenman. Read our review here .

blocks.text: Masterpiece of the week
An Elderly Man as Saint Paul by Rembrandt, probably 1659

blocks.alt: Elderly Man as Saint Paul, by Rembrandt, 1659
blocks.caption: Photograph: SuperStock/Alamy

blocks.text: You can see he’s wearing archaic garments and has religious trappings that identify him as the early Christian Paul, but all that slips your mind compared with this man’s incredibly real, suffering face. Paul, who set out some of the Church’s most severe views on matters including sexuality, doesn’t usually come across as anything like as doubtful or hesitant as this pensive soul. He is surrounded by the shadows of evening, or night, or death, and in his eyes you see a world of cares and regrets. Rembrandt has no respect for the conventions of art or storytelling that would make this a picture of Paul and allow us to move on after recognising that: instead he wants you to be shocked into recognition of the human predicament. You are held by this face, dragged behind the painting, into the man’s mind or soul or whatever we call the essence of the human. Nothing else, for Rembrandt, is worth making art about. National Gallery, London
